items.title: Irish central bank fines Coinbase unit €3.25 million
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: The Central Bank of Ireland fined crypto asset-trading platform Coinbase's Irish unit €3.25 million ($3.65 million) for breaching safeguarding and outsourcing obligations between 2020 and 2025, it said in a statement on Thursday.
items.body:
The Central Bank of Ireland fined crypto asset-trading platform Coinbase's Irish unit €3.25 million ($3.65 million) for breaching safeguarding and outsourcing obligations between 2020 and 2025, it said in a statement on Thursday.
The bank said the fine follows a settlement it reached with Coinbase Ireland on Wednesday, and came after rules related to protecting customer funds and maintaining confidence in the financial system were breached.
"Payment and e-money firms have a fundamental obligation to fully safeguard customers' funds," Central Bank Director of Enforcement Karen O'Leary said.
"The Central Bank has made its supervisory expectations in this regard clear: we have no tolerance for weaknesses in safeguarding arrangements."
A Coinbase spokesperson said it had self-reported the issues to the Central Bank and that "no customers suffered financial loss or were unable to access their funds as a result".
"These issues largely arose in the context of Coinbase taking steps to protect customers during periods of significant disruption," the spokesperson said in a statement.
Last year, the bank fined a Coinbase subsidiary [USN:L8N3WI1BC TEXT:"€21.5 million"] for breaching anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist transaction monitoring obligations.
($1 = 0.8915 euros)

items.title: Italien und Spanien beenden Streit über Einreisekontrollen
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: Fast drei Monate nach dem Migrantenansturm auf die spanische Nordafrika-Exklave Ceuta haben die Regierungen in Madrid und Rom ihren Streit über Einreisekontrollen beigelegt. Die Innenminister Spaniens und Italiens vereinbarten in einem Telefonat, die Aussetzung des Schengen-Abkommens nicht mehr zu verlängern, teilte das Innenministerium in Rom am Donnerstag mit. Damit werden Passkontrollen von Bürgern des jeweils anderen Landes wieder aufgehoben, die am 31. Juli zunächst Italien eingeführt hatte. Die Regierung unter Ministerpräsidentin Giorgia Meloni wollte damit sicherstellen, dass keine Migranten aus Ceuta nach Italien weiterreisen können.
items.body:
Fast drei Monate nach dem Migrantenansturm auf die spanische Nordafrika-Exklave Ceuta haben die Regierungen in Madrid und Rom ihren Streit über Einreisekontrollen beigelegt. Die Innenminister Spaniens und Italiens vereinbarten in einem Telefonat, die Aussetzung des Schengen-Abkommens nicht mehr zu verlängern, teilte das Innenministerium in Rom am Donnerstag mit. Damit werden Passkontrollen von Bürgern des jeweils anderen Landes wieder aufgehoben, die am 31. Juli zunächst Italien eingeführt hatte. Die Regierung unter Ministerpräsidentin Giorgia Meloni wollte damit sicherstellen, dass keine Migranten aus Ceuta nach Italien weiterreisen können.
Die Regierung in Madrid reagierte daraufhin mit ähnlichen Schritten und begann, aus Italien per Flugzeug oder Schiff einreisende Personen zu kontrollieren. Sie bezeichnete die italienischen Maßnahmen als ungerecht, diskriminierend für die spanische Bevölkerung und im Widerspruch zu den Interessen der EU. Beide Länder verlängerten die Einreisekontrollen, bis sie sich nun auf ein Ende der Maßnahmen einigten.
Das Innenministerium in Rom teilte am Donnerstag weiter mit, die Entscheidung sei nach einer sorgfältigen Prüfung der Lage getroffen worden. Sie werde von einem verstärkten Informationsaustausch begleitet, um die Sicherheit des gemeinsamen Schengen-Raums zu gewährleisten. Das Reisen ohne Kontrollen an den Binnengrenzen soll die Freizügigkeit in Europa fördern. Mittlerweile gehören dem 1985 in der luxemburgischen Kleinstadt Schengen vereinbarten Raum 29 Staaten an. Einige von ihnen, darunter auch Deutschland, hatten bereits vor längerer Zeit vorübergehende Grenzkontrollen eingeführt.

items.title: Dax-Konzern Qiagen vor Verkauf an Finanzinvestor EQT
items.author: Alexander Hübner, Patricia Weiss
items.creator: Alexander Hübner, Patricia Weiss
items.summary: Zum ersten Mal überhaupt steht ein Dax-Konzern vor dem Verkauf an einen Finanzinvestor. Die schwedische Beteiligungsfirma EQT bietet 10,8 Milliarden Euro für den deutsch-niederländischen Diagnostik-Spezialisten Qiagen. Vorstand und Aufsichtsrat erklärten in der Nacht zum Donnerstag, dass sich das Unternehmen mit Sitz in Venlo unter einem Finanzinvestor in der nächsten Wachstumsphase besser entwickeln könne als an der Börse. "Eine private Eigentümerstruktur gibt dem Management mehr Flexibilität, sich auf langfristige Wertschöpfung zu konzentrieren und seine strategischen Initiativen umzusetzen", sagte EQT-Partner Matteo Thun-Hohenstein der Nachrichtenagentur Reuters.
items.body:
Zum ersten Mal überhaupt steht ein Dax (.GDAXI) -Konzern vor dem Verkauf an einen Finanzinvestor. Die schwedische Beteiligungsfirma EQT (EQTAB.ST) bietet 10,8 Milliarden Euro für den deutsch-niederländischen Diagnostik-Spezialisten Qiagen (QIA.DE) . Vorstand und Aufsichtsrat erklärten in der Nacht zum Donnerstag, dass sich das Unternehmen mit Sitz in Venlo unter einem Finanzinvestor in der nächsten Wachstumsphase besser entwickeln könne als an der Börse. "Eine private Eigentümerstruktur gibt dem Management mehr Flexibilität, sich auf langfristige Wertschöpfung zu konzentrieren und seine strategischen Initiativen umzusetzen", sagte EQT-Partner Matteo Thun-Hohenstein der Nachrichtenagentur Reuters.
Die Übernahme kommt nur zustande, wenn sich EQT mehr als 50 Prozent der Qiagen-Aktien sichern kann. Danach - voraussichtlich Mitte 2027 - soll das Unternehmen von der Börse genommen werden. "Als privates Unternehmen können wir schneller handeln", sagte der neue Qiagen-Chef Jonathan Pratt. "Wir werden uns ansehen, wo wie Qiagen am besten unterstützen können. Wir sind da für alle Wege offen", ergänzte EQT-Partner Thun-Hohenstein. EQT baut dabei auf seine Erfahrung in der Gesundheitsbranche, auf der in den vergangenen zehn Jahren der Schwerpunkt der Investments des Finanzinvestors lag.
Qiagen wurde 1984 in Düsseldorf gegründet und ist seit 1997 an der Frankfurter Börse notiert. Das auf Tests zum Nachweis von Krankheiten und auf Laborgeräte spezialisierte Unternehmen beschäftigt 5500 Mitarbeiter an über 35 Standorten weltweit. "Wir beobachten seit vielen Jahren den Erfolg von Qiagen. Das Unternehmen hat einen hervorragenden Ruf", sagte Thun-Hohenstein. "Wir sind stolz, Teil dieser Geschichte zu werden."
Dax-Unternehmen galten als Übernahmeziel für Private Equity lange Zeit als zu groß, weil die Beteiligungsfirmen das Geld ihrer Anleger lieber breiter streuen. Zuletzt hatten sie in Deutschland vor allem kleinere Unternehmen ins Visier genommen, die sie an der Börse für unterbewertet hielten. Doch angesichts größerer Fonds und mit Hilfe von Co-Investoren für einzelne Investments ist die finanzielle Schlagkraft der größten Finanzinvestoren gewachsen. EQT hat sich für die Übernahme zwei finanzkräftige Geldgeber an Bord geholt, die jeweils Minderheitsanteile übernehmen wollen: den Staatsfonds von Abu Dhabi, ADIA, und die kanadische Pensionskasse CPP Investments.
QIAGEN-AKTIE LEGT UM 5,5 PROZENT ZU EQT stach mit der Offerte Insidern zufolge unter anderem den US-Rivalen KKR (KKR.N) aus. Qiagen erklärte, man habe auch mit Interessenten aus der Branche gesprochen. Das Angebot über 46,50 Euro je Aktie liegt zwar nur knapp neun Prozent über dem Xetra-Schlusskurs vom Mittwoch. Die Qiagen-Aktie war aber schon seit Monaten von Hoffnungen auf eine Übernahme getrieben worden. Im Vergleich zum Kurs von Anfang Juli, als erstmals über Interesse von Finanzinvestoren berichtet wurde, bedeute die Offerte einen Aufschlag von 40 Prozent, rechneten Qiagen und EQT vor. An der Frankfurter Börse legten die Papiere am Donnerstag 5,5 Prozent auf 45,17 Euro zu.
In einer Investmentvereinbarung mit Qiagen hat der künftige Eigentümer nach eigenen Angaben langfristige Zusagen in Bezug auf die Strategie, die wichtigsten Marken, die Forschungs- und Entwicklungsaktivitäten, die Mitarbeiter und die Finanzierungsstruktur gemacht. Qiagen werde auch weiterhin unter der eigenen Marke aktiv sein.
THERMO FISHER BOT VOR SECHS JAHREN MEHR Um Qiagen ranken sich seit Jahren Übernahmespekulationen. Am konkretesten war ein Verkauf 2020 gewesen, als der US-Laborausrüster Thermo Fisher (TMO.N) rund 11,3 Milliarden Euro bot. Doch die Übernahme scheiterte am Widerstand der Aktionäre, die die Offerte angesichts der damals boomenden Nachfrage nach Corona-Tests für zu niedrig hielten. Auch der Rivale Biomerieux (BIOX.PA) aus Frankreich, der US-Diagnostikspezialist Quidel und der US-Wettbewerber Bio-Rad (BIO.N) wurden schon als mögliche Interessenten gehandelt.
Das Geschäft von Qiagen läuft: Im dritten Quartal lagen die Zahlen über den eigenen Erwartungen. Der Umsatz kletterte um knapp drei Prozent auf 548 Millionen Dollar. Im August hatte das Management nur ein Plus von ein bis zwei Prozent in Aussicht gestellt. Auch der bereinigte Gewinn je Aktie übertraf mit 65 Cent die Prognose von mindestens 62 Cent.

items.title: Chemicals maker Dow beats third-quarter profit estimates
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: Dow Inc beat Wall Street estimates for third-quarter adjusted profit on Thursday, helped by cost-cutting measures and higher prices driven by a supply shortage due to the Middle East conflict.
items.body:
Dow Inc (DOW.N) beat Wall Street estimates for third-quarter adjusted profit on Thursday, helped by cost-cutting measures and higher prices driven by a supply shortage due to the Middle East conflict.
The closure of the Strait of Hormuz following the escalation of the Iran conflict in late February has disrupted oil and petrochemical flows, tightening global chemical supplies and driving a [USN:L4N40C10N TEXT:"sharp increase"] in plastics and polymer prices.
Dow has been [USN:L4N3M016I TEXT:"reviewing"] non-producing assets across its portfolio, including power and steam facilities and pipelines, as the chemical industry grapples with higher feedstock and energy costs amid weak demand in key markets.
Third-quarter net sales from its packaging and specialty plastics segment rose over 18% to $5.8 billion from a year ago.
The Michigan-based company reported an adjusted profit of 71 cents per share for the quarter ended September 30, compared with analysts' average estimate of 64 cents, according to data compiled by LSEG.
items.raw_description: Dow Inc beat Wall Street estimates for third-quarter adjusted profit on Thursday, helped by cost-cutting measures and higher prices driven by a supply shortage due to the Middle East conflict.

items.title: Lockheed, Pentagon strike initial deal to produce 850 F-35 jets
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: Lockheed Martin has entered an initial production and sustainment agreement with the Department of Defense for 850 F-35 Lightning II fighter jet over the next 10 years, the defense contractor said on Thursday.
items.body:
Lockheed Martin (LMT.N) has entered an initial production and sustainment agreement with the Department of Defense for 850 F-35 Lightning II fighter jet over the next 10 years, the defense contractor said on Thursday.
The F-35, built with stealth technology that allows it to evade enemy detection, is considered the world's most advanced fighter jet and is at the core of Lockheed's aeronautics division that forms close to 40% of its quarterly revenue.
Under the agreement with the Department of Defense, which US President Donald Trump calls the Department of War, Lockheed aims to maintain annual production at 156 aircraft.
The agreement does not constitute an order but is counted as a prearranged long-term contract.
"If granted multi-year authority in the coming months, the F-35 Joint Program Office and Lockheed Martin will work to finalize contract terms, pricing and schedules through a formal contract award," the company said.
The agreement also covers international orders for the F-35, as well as initial spares and modification kits, Arlington-based Lockheed said in a statement.
Lockheed and its peers across the US have benefited from increased global defense spending as geopolitical conflicts remain unabated.
Lockheed estimates the agreement will support 317,000 US jobs and generate nearly $79 billion in annual economic activity over the next decade.
It also expects the arrangement to lower production costs and ease supply-chain constraints from raw materials to finished parts.

items.title: RBI will sich nach Gerichtssieg Strabag-Milliardenpaket sichern
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: Die Raiffeisen Bank International (RBI) ist im Ringen um ein Aktienpaket am Baukonzern Strabag einen juristischen Schritt weiter. Ein vom Wiener Landesgericht für Zivilrechtssachen erlassenes Versäumnisurteil gegen die russische Gesellschaft Rasperia habe am Donnerstag Rechtskraft erlangt, teilte die Bank mit. Die RBI werde nun bei der österreichischen Finanzmarktaufsicht (FMA) die Freigabe der Strabag-Aktien beantragen. Damit solle ein Schadenersatzanspruch in Höhe von 3,15 Milliarden Euro gegen Rasperia vollstreckt werden.
items.body:
Die Raiffeisen Bank International (RBI) (RBIV.VI) ist im Ringen um ein Aktienpaket am Baukonzern Strabag (STRV.VI) einen juristischen Schritt weiter. Ein vom Wiener Landesgericht für Zivilrechtssachen erlassenes Versäumnisurteil gegen die russische Gesellschaft Rasperia habe am Donnerstag Rechtskraft erlangt, teilte die Bank mit. Die RBI werde nun bei der österreichischen Finanzmarktaufsicht (FMA) die Freigabe der Strabag-Aktien beantragen. Damit solle ein Schadenersatzanspruch in Höhe von 3,15 Milliarden Euro gegen Rasperia vollstreckt werden.
Die Klage in Wien zog jedoch eine prompte Reaktion aus Russland nach sich. Wie am Dienstag bekannt wurde, verurteilte ein russisches Gericht die dortige RBI-Tochter zu einer Strafzahlung von 342 Millionen Euro an Rasperia. Für die RBI sei dies eine "erwartbare Folge" gewesen. Ein russisches Gericht hatte der Bank zwar eine Schadenersatzklage in Österreich erlaubt, diese jedoch auf einen Streitwert von 2,85 Milliarden Euro begrenzt. Die RBI klagte in Wien jedoch 3,15 Milliarden Euro ein, die in Russland verhängte Strafe entspricht dem Mehrbetrag zuzüglich Gerichtsgebühren.
Hintergrund der Klage in Wien ist ein Urteil aus dem Frühjahr 2025. Damals hatte ein russisches Gericht die russische RBI-Tochter zur Zahlung von rund 2,4 Milliarden Euro an Rasperia verurteilt. Der Rechtsstreit hatte sich daran entzündet, dass die Strabag wegen der EU-Sanktionen gegen den ursprünglichen Aktionär, den Oligarchen Oleg Deripaska, keine Dividenden an Rasperia auszahlen durfte. Da die Strabag in Russland keine Vermögenswerte besitzt, hatte Rasperia daraufhin die dortige RBI-Tochter verklagt. Mit dem nun rechtskräftigen Urteil in Wien will die RBI diesen in Russland entstandenen Schaden kompensieren und auf die in Österreich eingefrorenen Vermögenswerte von Rasperia zugreifen.
Bei den eingefrorenen Vermögenswerten handelt es sich um ein Paket von 28,5 Millionen Strabag-Aktien sowie um Dividenden und eine Barausschüttung. Wer heute hinter Rasperia steht, ist unklar. Die RBI ist die größte westliche Bank, die noch in Russland tätig ist, und steht unter Druck der Europäischen Zentralbank, ihr dortiges Geschäft deutlich zurückzufahren.

items.title: High gas prices strain Detroit's hungry and food banks ahead of midterm elections
items.author: Heather Schlitz
items.creator: Heather Schlitz
items.summary: A neatly packed cardboard box of pasta, dry beans, canned goods and powdered milk made Tonya King cry.
items.body:
A neatly packed cardboard box of pasta, dry beans, canned goods and powdered milk made Tonya King cry.
“I’ve been waiting for this,” said King, a 65-year-old Detroit grandmother, her voice cracking while tears streamed down her face. “Finally, my daughter called me and said ‘he’s coming.'"
King had been waiting for Frank Kubik, a director at the Focus: Hope nonprofit food program, who arrived with the box of food that will feed her household of six for two weeks. The food bank caters mostly to lower-income seniors on fixed incomes, many of whom can no longer afford to pick up food donations because of higher gas prices and need more assistance as grocery prices increase.
The need for food assistance is growing across the United States just as it is becoming costlier for food banks to deliver it. Soaring diesel prices driven up by the US-led war on Iran have raised delivery costs for food while inflation and cuts in federal food assistance have increased demand from struggling Americans.
The cost of living has become a central concern for voters weighing their choices in the US Senate race in Michigan, one of several competitive races in the [USN:L1N4600TJ TEXT:"November 3 midterm elections"] that could decide whether Democrats can retake control of the US Senate. Nearly half of registered voters nationwide cited the cost of living as the most important factor in their midterm vote, according to a [USN:L6N46017L TEXT:"recent Reuters/Ipsos poll."]
King plans to vote for Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed, an epidemiologist and former director of Detroit's health department, hoping he will address the rising cost of living and healthcare, two issues at the center of his campaign. His Republican rival, Mike Rogers, has called for suspending state and federal gas taxes and introducing tax cuts to address the issue of affordability.
“I have to decide between my seizure medication and my diabetes medication,” King said. “We need someone to come in and change things.”
For King, food is just the first in a long line of necessities she can’t afford as high gas prices cut into what little income her family gets from government assistance.
Their furnace is broken, and the family can’t afford to fix it as winter looms. The house smells of urine – there hasn’t been running water for over a month and King uses a bedpan as cerebral palsy has made her immobile. The gaping hole in the floorboards that shows the basement, exposed window frame where pink insulation peeks through and a crooked porch are the lowest on her list of priorities.
“I was having to hold myself back from tears,” Kubik said as he walked back to his car.
PRESSURE NATIONWIDE Focus: Hope now delivers 1,300 monthly food boxes to low-income seniors, up from 800 at the start of the year, as rising gas prices make it harder for them to reach food distribution points.
Food pantries across the nation are feeling the strain.
In California, Central California Food Bank co-CEO Kym Dildine said the food bank’s spending on diesel rose 61% from July through September, compared to the same period a year ago.
“That equates to about a quarter million meals that we could have provided in the community now being redirected to fuel costs,” she said. The food bank is the largest hunger relief organization in the region and provides food to charities that feed more than 300,000 people every month.
“Our donors also are being pinched at the pump. Food banks rely on $25 to $250 donations and it’s those donors who are being most impacted by escalating fuel prices,” said Dildine.
At the same time, retailers who previously may have covered transportation expenses for the food they donate are now either sharing the cost or asking food banks to shoulder it, she said.
The Greater Chicago Food Depository, one of the city’s largest food banks, is shifting toward providing cheaper foods, such as eggs, to offset rising fuel costs that are straining its own budget, a spokesperson said.
Cuts to government benefits for lower-income households have added yet another strain to food banks and the hungry. Nationwide, [USN:L6N4240XG TEXT:"more than 4.7 million people"] have lost their Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits, also known as food stamps, since President Donald Trump’s signature tax and spending law took effect last year.
Jona Berry, an 84-year-old retired store clerk in Detroit who also received a food box from Focus: Hope, said the boxes have helped her get by on her fixed income as groceries get more expensive.
"I manage," she said. "I know how to stretch stuff."
items.raw_description: A neatly packed cardboard box of pasta, dry beans, canned goods and powdered milk made Tonya King cry.

items.title: How would a Netanyahu election loss change Israel's policies toward the Palestinians?
items.author: Lina Obeid, Tamar Uriel-Beeri
items.creator: Lina Obeid, Tamar Uriel-Beeri
items.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his main opponent Gadi Eisenkot both oppose an independent Palestinian state, meaning next week's election is unlikely to produce a sweeping shift in policies that have hampered a decades-old peace process.
items.body:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his main opponent Gadi Eisenkot both oppose an independent Palestinian state, meaning next week's election is unlikely to produce a sweeping shift in policies that have hampered a decades-old peace process.
Three years since the Hamas-led October 7 attacks, they also share hawkish positions towards Gaza, saying they would resume the war there if the militant group, whose founding charter calls for Israel's destruction, doesn't disarm.
But they differ on their positions on settlements in the occupied West Bank, and are likely to rely on different coalition partners to form governments, which could broadly set the country on diverging paths.
Here's a look at the candidates' views on the conflict with the Palestinians:
WEST BANK SETTLEMENTS Hundreds of thousands of Israelis live in the West Bank, settling in territory Israel captured in a 1967 war, a practice nearly all countries consider illegal under international law, although Israel disputes this.
Netanyahu has presided over a rapid expansion of settlements, including small outposts in parts of the West Bank reserved for civil administration by the Palestinian Authority, where settlements are illegal under Israel's own laws. Settlers have increasingly attacked Palestinians, and critics say the government has turned a blind eye to such violence.
Eisenkot favours settlement in principle, but says that it should comply with Israeli law. He opposes settlements built without authorisation, would dismantle outposts in areas where they are forbidden, and has pledged to prevent violence by settlers against Palestinians.
He also opposes a decision by the Netanyahu government to build in territory known as [USN:L2N3UY0PU TEXT:"E1"], which would bisect the West Bank and cut it off from East Jerusalem, which settlers say is intended to "bury" the possibility of a Palestinian state.
PALESTINIAN SELF-RULE In a sign of how far Israeli politics has shifted to the right, Netanyahu and Eisenkot, along with the leaders of nearly all other Jewish-led parties, oppose the establishment of a future independent Palestinian state alongside Israel.
This effectively repudiates the "two-state solution" that underpinned international peace negotiations for generations.
Netanyahu and Eisenkot both say Israel must retain ultimate security control over all territory between the Jordan River and Mediterranean Sea.
There are, however, differences in their emphasis. Eisenkot's position on limiting settlements in the West Bank would reserve territory where Palestinians now exercise civil self rule. Netanyahu's coalition includes parties that openly call for Israel to fully annex occupied Palestinian land.
GAZA Three years since Hamas-led fighters attacked southern Israel prompting an Israeli invasion of the Gaza Strip, and a year since a US-brokered ceasefire ended major combat there, Israeli troops now control around two-thirds of the enclave.
Nearly the entire population of more than 2 million Palestinians lives in the remaining third, mainly in tents or damaged buildings, still under the full political control of Hamas. US-brokered talks have so far failed to agree terms for Hamas to disarm, Israel to withdraw and reconstruction to begin under international auspices.
Both Eisenkot and Netanyahu say Israeli troops will not withdraw from Gaza until Hamas is disarmed, and that Israel is prepared to restart fighting to achieve this.
Eisenkot says the continued rule of Hamas in Gaza is a profound failure, and that within 18 months of taking office he would ensure that the Hamas administration had been replaced, either through a US-brokered plan or through military force.
COALITION PARTNERS Netanyahu's governing coalition now includes far-right Jewish nationalist groups led by settler activists Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, who support full annexation of Palestinian land and are under sanctions in several Western countries for promoting settler violence.
Netanyahu also relies on ultra-Orthodox parties that seek exemptions from military service for Jewish religious students.
Opposition parties likely to be courted by Eisenkot for a future coalition to unseat Netanyahu include several right-wing groups, but none with leaders as extreme as Smotrich or Ben-Gvir. His supporters are mainly opposed to the military exemption for religious students, which probably rules out an alliance with the ultra-Orthodox.
To unseat Netanyahu, Eisenkot is likely to require the support of the Democrats, which include the rump of the centre-left Labour Party that dominated Israeli politics for generations but has dwindled as the country has shifted to the right. The Democrats are now the only prominent Jewish-led party that supports a two-state solution.
Eisenkot and Netanyahu have both said they would not form a government with parties primarily representing Israeli citizens of Palestinian descent, who comprise around a fifth of the population.
items.raw_description: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his main opponent Gadi Eisenkot both oppose an independent Palestinian state, meaning next week's election is unlikely to produce a sweeping shift in policies that have hampered a decades-old peace process.

items.title: Trump heads to Iowa as Republicans fight for seats in longtime stronghold
items.author: Nandita Bose
items.creator: Nandita Bose
items.summary: President Donald Trump heads to Iowa on Thursday to shore up Republicans in a state he won by 13 percentage points two years ago, but where his weakened standing and voter anxiety over his policies have complicated the party's prospects in the November 3 midterm elections.
items.body:
President Donald Trump heads to Iowa on Thursday to shore up Republicans in a state he won by 13 percentage points two years ago, but where his weakened standing and voter anxiety over his policies have complicated the party's prospects in the November 3 midterm elections.
Trump will hold a rally in Sioux City as Republicans defend a Senate seat, three House districts and the governor's office, giving Democrats an opening after years of Republican gains.
Some Republicans Trump is trying to help have [USN:L1N45D0Y8 TEXT:"broken with him"] over the Iran war, as higher fuel and grocery prices deepen voters' economic worries.
Republican Representative Ashley Hinson, in a close Senate race against Democratic state Representative Josh Turek, has called for an "immediate end" to the war, saying Iowans should not bear higher fuel or grocery prices because of it.
Republican Representatives Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Zach Nunn, facing difficult reelection races, joined Democrats last month in voting to limit Trump's war powers in Iran.
Democrat Rob Sand leads Republican Zach Lahn in recent polling for governor, while Democrats are targeting an open House seat in Iowa's second congressional district.
Republican losses would be a setback for Trump in a state where his popularity helped the party build a commanding advantage. The Senate and House races could help decide control of Congress, shaping his ability to advance his agenda during his final two years.
Republicans also worry about rural voters who powered Trump's Iowa victories, with farmers facing higher costs and trade uncertainty. A Marist poll this month found 42% of likely voters said their finances had worsened over the past year, including more than half of independents. Thirty-five percent viewed their vote as a vote against Trump, versus 21% who saw it as a vote for him.
Iowa is part of Trump's push through states Republicans usually expect to win. He [USN:L1N4650ZT TEXT:"campaigned"] in Kansas on Monday for Republican Senator Roger Marshall and traveled [USN:L1N4660VQ TEXT:"to South Carolina"] on Wednesday to support Republican Senator Darline Graham.
Trump is trying to turn out supporters who back him in presidential contests but may stay home when he is not on the ballot. He has urged them to vote as though he were running.
His campaign swing comes as his approval rating has fallen to 31%, the lowest of either presidential term, according to a [USN:L6N465159 TEXT:"Reuters/Ipsos poll"] released Monday. The survey found 68% of Americans disapproved of his handling of the economy.
At recent rallies, his economic message has largely avoided the financial pressures facing many Americans. The Iran war has driven up gas prices, compounding broader cost-of-living concerns, while Trump has repeatedly promised prices will fall when the conflict ends.
Behind the scenes, Trump has [USN:L4N4612B3 TEXT:"questioned"] campaign spending, criticized redistricting efforts and second-guessed candidate choices, according to people familiar with the matter. White House spokesman Davis Ingle rejected the people's characterizations, saying they were "armchair experts peddling their baseless speculation." Publicly, Trump has noted the tendency of a president's party to lose seats in midterm elections.
Trump is scheduled to return to Iowa on November 1, two days before Election Day.

items.title: UK factory output expected to stabilise, CBI survey shows
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: Output in Britain's manufacturing sector is expected to stabilise in the next three months despite a dip in orders in October, a Confederation of British Industry survey showed on Thursday.
items.body:
Output in Britain's manufacturing sector is expected to stabilise in the next three months despite a dip in orders in October, a Confederation of British Industry survey showed on Thursday.
The reading of -1 in the CBI's volume of output gauge for the next three months came after a run of flat or falling production that began in mid-2022.
"But with orders still falling and labour shortages picking up, significant challenges remain," CBI senior economist Cameron Martin said.
"Stubbornly high costs are also squeezing profitability while deteriorating competitiveness and fragile business confidence continue to weigh on investment decisions."
Official data has shown solid growth in Britain's manufacturing output this year.
• The CBI's monthly order books balance dropped to -32 in October from -9 in September
• The survey's quarterly gauge of expectations for output in the months ahead improved to -1 from -30 in July
• The quarterly measure of expected domestic prices rose to +24 from +11

items.title: International Criminal Court wins EU's 2026 Sakharov prize
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: The International Criminal Court has been awarded the European Union's 2026 Sakharov Prize, the EU's top prize regarding human rights work.
items.body:
The International Criminal Court has been awarded the European Union's 2026 Sakharov Prize, the EU's top prize regarding human rights work.
The prize is the second international recognition for the war crimes tribunal this month, and comes within two weeks after US President Donald Trump announced [USN:L8N45U28I TEXT:"sanctions"] against the court.
That announcement was made hours after former ICC judge [USN:L8N45V0JG TEXT:"Navi Pillay"] was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize, which was widely seen as a show of support for the embattled court.
The Hague-based ICC has long been a target of US President Donald Trump, whose [USN:L6N45G1BM TEXT:"campaign against it has escalated"] since the court announced arrest warrants against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former defence minister last year.
The EU prize, named after the late Soviet dissident Andrei Sakharov, has been awarded annually since 1988 to individuals and orgaizations defending human rights and freedoms.

items.title: Trotz neuer US-Friedensinitiative - Schwere Luftangriffe auf Kiew und Moskau
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: Russland und die Ukraine haben sich ungeachtet neuer US-Vermittlungsbemühungen gegenseitig mit schweren Luftangriffen überzogen, bei denen am Donnerstag drei Menschen getötet wurden. Bei russischen Raketenangriffen auf Kiew und andere Landesteile starben nach ukrainischen Angaben zwei Menschen, 34 weitere wurden verletzt. Die Ukraine griff Ziele in Russland mit Drohnen an. Dabei wurde in der Grenzregion Belgorod ein Mensch getötet, nahe Moskau gab es zwei Verletzte.
items.body:
Russland und die Ukraine haben sich ungeachtet neuer US-Vermittlungsbemühungen gegenseitig mit schweren Luftangriffen überzogen, bei denen am Donnerstag drei Menschen getötet wurden. Bei russischen Raketenangriffen auf Kiew und andere Landesteile starben nach ukrainischen Angaben zwei Menschen, 34 weitere wurden verletzt. Die Ukraine griff Ziele in Russland mit Drohnen an. Dabei wurde in der Grenzregion Belgorod ein Mensch getötet, nahe Moskau gab es zwei Verletzte.
Die Angriffe ereigneten sich kurz nach den Gesprächen des US-Sondergesandten Steve Witkoff mit dem russischen Präsidenten Wladimir Putin in St. Petersburg am Mittwoch und dem ukrainischen Präsidenten Wolodymyr Selenskyj am Dienstag in Oslo. Russland erklärte sich danach bereit, die von den USA vermittelten Gespräche mit der Ukraine im kommenden Monat wieder aufzunehmen.
Nach Angaben Selenskyjs feuerte Russland seit Dienstagabend in drei Wellen insgesamt 21 ballistische Raketen ab. Unter den Verletzten in der Ukraine seien auch fünf Kinder. Zudem habe Russland einen massiven Angriff auf die Hafeninfrastruktur in der Region Odessa sowie auf Schiffe der ukrainischen Marine ausgeführt. Auf russischer Seite seien in der Nacht insgesamt 630 ukrainische Drohnen in Richtung Moskau gesteuert worden, teilte Bürgermeister Sergej Sobjanin mit. Die meisten davon seien jedoch in großer Entfernung abgeschossen worden.
Die Angriffe überschatteten die diplomatischen Bemühungen des US-Gesandten Witkoff. Dieser hatte Putin am Mittwoch für die Freilassung des inhaftierten US-Bürgers Stephen Hubbard gedankt und den Kreml-Chef dabei als "Humanisten" bezeichnet. Dies stieß in Kiew auf scharfe Kritik. "Drei Wellen ballistischer Raketen wurden seit gestern Abend von russischen 'Humanisten' auf Kiew abgefeuert", schrieb Selenskyj auf der Online-Plattform X. "Leider wurden zahlreiche Ziele in der Stadt getroffen und beschädigt."
"EINIGE NEUE NUANCEN" Trotz der anhaltenden Angriffe gibt es diplomatische Signale. Selenskyj äußerte die Hoffnung, dass die Verhandlungen Anfang November stattfinden könnten. Es wären die ersten Gespräche dieser Art seit Februar. Während Witkoff nach Treffen mit Selenskyj sowie Vertretern der EU und der Nato in Oslo von einer "gewissen Dynamik" sprach, gab sich der Kreml zurückhaltender. "Die Amerikaner haben einige neue Nuancen wahrgenommen und uns davon berichtet. Aber diese Nuancen sind für uns, gelinde gesagt, nicht völlig zufriedenstellend", sagte Kreml-Berater Juri Uschakow.
Einem Insider zufolge sahen die in Oslo ausgearbeiteten Vorschläge vor, dass die Ukraine den gesamten Donbass an Russland abtritt und im Gegenzug Sicherheitsgarantien der Nato erhält. Russland lehnt jedoch jegliche westliche Militärpräsenz in der Ukraine nach einem Ende des Konflikts ab. Der völkerrechtswidrige russische Angriffskrieg dauert nun schon mehr als viereinhalb Jahre an. Da die Frontlinien weitgehend erstarrt sind, haben beide Seiten in diesem Jahr ihre Luftangriffe auf Ziele wie Raffinerien, Stromnetze und Depots intensiviert. Bisherige Verhandlungsrunden in Istanbul, Abu Dhabi und Genf brachten keinen Durchbruch.

items.title: Polymarket, Kalshi expand political donations as firms face state, federal scrutiny
items.author: Douglas Gillison
items.creator: Douglas Gillison
items.summary: Prediction market operators Kalshi, Polymarket and their founders have given at least $5 million combined to Republican and Democratic political groups this election cycle, according to campaign finance records and a private remittance document seen by Reuters.
items.body:
Prediction market operators Kalshi, Polymarket and their founders have given at least $5 million combined to Republican and Democratic political groups this election cycle, according to campaign finance records and a private remittance document seen by Reuters.
The spending includes a previously unreported $1 million donation Polymarket made to a Democratic nonprofit that does not disclose its donors, the remittance document shows.
Though a fraction of the [USN:L1N4310KM TEXT:"money spent by similar industries such as crypto"] and [USN:L6N43Q0T7 TEXT:"sports betting"], the companies' $5 million outlay is a sharp increase on the 2024 cycle, marking their first significant foray into political giving.
The pair have so far slightly favored Republicans, who received $2.7 million, with Democrats taking the remainder. Just over a third of the total cash went to state-level groups backing candidates for governor, attorney general and state legislatures, according to an analysis by the Center for Political Accountability (CPA), a transparency nonprofit.
The spending surge comes as both companies [USN:L6N45G0XO TEXT:"battle state efforts to regulate their wagers as gambling"], and as they face growing scrutiny from federal lawmakers worried that prediction markets are spawning insider trading and undermining national security.
"We have an industry where we're kind of figuring out the regulations on the fly," said David Primo, a professor of political science at the University of Rochester in New York.
"If you're not engaging with these politicians, other people are going to be writing these regulations, and that could be an existential threat to these companies," he said.
In a statement, Kalshi's head of federal government relations, John Bivona, said that by Election Day the company's full disclosures would show that its donations were roughly evenly distributed across both parties.
"Regulation that keeps prediction markets safe for consumers and allows them to grow in America isn't a partisan issue," he added.
A Polymarket spokesperson did not address questions about the company's donations but said in an email: "We engage with all sides of the debate and welcome conversations with anyone who wants to learn more about our platform."
POLYMARKET CEO COPLAN STARTS GIVING TO REPUBLICANS Prediction markets allow wagers on an array of events, including sports games, elections and government announcements. Kalshi and Polymarket rose to prominence in 2024 when they bucked traditional opinion polls in [USN:L1N3M00OE TEXT:"signaling that President Donald Trump"], a Republican, would win the election.
Trump's administration has generally supported the industry, although a handful of congressional Republicans have raised concerns about election betting. Democrats, meanwhile, have introduced multiple bills aimed at restricting prediction wagers.
Polymarket Chief Executive Shayne Coplan, who previously donated almost exclusively to Democrats, has broadened his giving this cycle. Campaign finance records show that he and Polymarket have directed roughly $1.3 million to Republican committees and candidates, while also supporting Democratic groups.
According to the remittance document seen by Reuters, Blockratize Inc, which operates as Polymarket, this summer transferred $1 million to House Majority Forward, a nonprofit that works to elect Democrats. Companies frequently donate via such tax-exempt "dark-money" organizations, which are not required to disclose their donors.
Polymarket and Coplan gave the roughly $1.3 million combined to the Republican National Committee, as well as a super political action committee, or PAC, supporting House Republicans, and V-PAC, a super PAC which supports Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy.
Representatives for House Majority Forward and the Republican fundraising vehicles either declined to comment or did not respond to requests for comment.
Reuters could not identify any political contributions by Kalshi founders Luana Lopes Lara and Tarek Mansour in publicly available campaign finance records for previous cycles. As of early October, they had given at least $1 million, about 72% of which went to Republican causes and candidates, campaign finance records show.
COMPANIES GIVE TO STATE GROUPS AMID LEGAL FIGHT State gaming authorities, attorneys general and Native American tribes have sued to block Kalshi, Polymarket and others from offering sports bets, arguing that such wagers are gambling and subject to stringent state oversight. The companies say their wagers [USN:L6N43T15B TEXT:"are financial instruments"] overseen by federal agencies.
This cycle, the companies began donating to groups that back state-level candidates who could determine how that fight unfolds, with spending accelerating over the past 12 months and so far marginally favoring Democrats, the CPA data shows.
Kalshi has so far given nearly $1.5 million to such groups, split roughly evenly across both parties. Polymarket has so far given nearly $250,000 to two Democratic groups and one Republican group, the data shows.
Jeanne Hanna, vice president for research at CPA, said the slight tilt toward Democratic groups could reflect an expectation that the party is poised for greater success at the state level this election cycle. In addition to funding campaigns, such state-level groups also allow companies to establish rapport with policymakers, she said.
"There definitely is a membership structure in which larger contributions get you greater access," she added.

FAST

Oct 22 : Meta Platforms has a strong basis for arguing that the $25 billion penalty New Mexico secured this week in a case stemming from allegations the firm mishandled user data should be reduced on appeal, legal experts said. 
The judgment was one of the largest state verdicts against a company in US history. It came after a jury found Meta misled consumers about who had access to their data in the wake of revelations that Cambridge Analytica, a political consulting firm involved in President Donald Trump's 2016 presidential campaign, had harvested personal data from millions of Facebook users. 
New Mexico said state law allowed for a penalty of up to $5,000 for each time someone in the state may have seen an allegedly misleading statement from Meta. Experts said the company would likely argue that Judge Francis Mathew should only have considered people who actually saw the statements.  
"The most vulnerable basis on appeal is going to be the question about whether a violation is going to count, even in the absence of any proof that a particular person saw one of these misrepresentations or relied on them to their detriment," said Peter Ormerod, a law professor at Villanova University.

C.J. Mahoney, Meta's chief legal officer, said the company is confident it will win on appeal. The company is expected to appeal the underlying jury verdict and the penalty.
Meta has previously said that it does not sell user data and that New Mexico did not prove any consumer had actually been misled and that a penalty in the billions of dollars would risk violating its constitutional rights to due process and protection from excessive fines. 
New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said on Wednesday he expected Meta to appeal the judgment and the state stood ready to defend its legal position. He did not immediately respond to a request for further comment.
JURY FOUND 43 MILLION VIOLATIONS
New Mexico's attorney general sued Meta in 2021, alleging that the company lied to Facebook users about who had access to their data, how the company handled hate speech and misinformation posted on the platform, and other internal policies. 
Jurors on September 25 found that 26 of 29 statements made by the company and its leadership on those issues were misleading. Multiplying those statements by their potential audience within New Mexico, the jury said the company had committed more than 43 million violations of the state’s consumer protection laws. The state had 1.4 million active Facebook users and a population of 2.1 million as of 2020. 
Mathew said in his ruling on Wednesday that a penalty of more than $219 billion would be justified under state law, which allows a $5,000 penalty for each violation, but he reduced the amount.
The state had urged Mathew to award the state between $35 billion and $40 billion, while Meta said penalties of no more than $3.45 billion were warranted. 
Ormerod said that even if the company's appeals in state courts fail, Meta could argue to the US Supreme Court that the penalty violated its rights under the US Constitution to due process and against excessive fines. 
The size of the penalty on its own does not mean it will be overturned, given the New Mexico law allowing for penalties for each willful violation, said Daryl Lim, a professor at Penn State Dickinson Law. 
But it seems implausible that Meta was really responsible for so much financial harm, a sign the penalty may be unjust, said Eric Goldman, a professor at Santa Clara University School of Law.
"It felt like there was a lot of duplicative counting in the calculations," Goldman said. "How many times can a single person be duped by the same entity?" 

Source: Reuters

items.title: As Trump's support slips, white evangelicals remain his Republican bedrock
items.author: Nathan Layne, Julio-Cesar Chavez, Jason Lange
items.creator: Nathan Layne, Julio-Cesar Chavez, Jason Lange
items.summary: President Donald Trump is losing ground among many of the voters who returned him to the White House in 2024. But Reuters/Ipsos polling and interviews with white evangelical Christians show they remain his most reliable constituency and could prove crucial in the November 3 midterm elections.
items.body:
President Donald Trump is losing ground among many of the voters who returned him to the White House in 2024. But Reuters/Ipsos polling and interviews with white evangelical Christians show they remain his most reliable constituency and could prove crucial in the November 3 midterm elections .
With Republicans on the defensive amid record-low approval ratings for Trump, strong evangelical turnout could help the party limit losses driven by voter frustration over the cost of living and the war in Iran .
That loyalty was on display last week at Village Church, an evangelical congregation in Blythewood, South Carolina, where hundreds of worshippers gathered for a weekly “Bible and Politics” sermon by Pastor Erik Estep. The backdrop: an unexpectedly competitive race for a Republican-held US Senate seat.
Speaking in the main worship hall, framed by a giant video screen and concert-style lighting, Estep did not endorse a candidate or party. But as he spoke against gambling, following sermons on abortion and socialism, he urged his predominantly white parishioners to view politics through a biblical lens.
"I believe the church is the bulwark of truth for our nation," Estep said from the stage. "And it will take people like you and churches like this church to protect this nation spiritually and morally."
The message resonated with Karen Whiting, a 72-year-old retired pharmaceutical executive who plans to vote for Republican Darline Graham over Annie Andrews, the Democrat. Graham was appointed by the governor to fill the seat of her late brother, [USN:FWN43C0M3 TEXT:"Senator Lindsey Graham"].
Whiting cited concerns that Democrats would allow transgender girls and women to compete in female sports, echoing other white evangelicals Reuters interviewed in South Carolina last week who prioritized social and religious issues over economic concerns .
"I’m voting for biblical principles, and I do not believe the Democratic Party stands for biblical principles,” Whiting said. “Without God, this country’s going to fail.”
If visitors to Village Church needed more explicit guidance on how to vote, a candidate guide available in the church lobby left little doubt. Produced by the conservative Christian advocacy group Palmetto Family Council and distributed to churches across South Carolina, it awarded Graham green check marks on all seven issues it rated, including restrictions on abortion medication and gender-affirming care, while Andrews received mostly red X's.
Andrews offered a different reading of evangelical voters’ priorities. In a statement to Reuters, she said she had visited evangelical churches and met voters of various faiths, political persuasions and backgrounds, finding that they were chiefly concerned about the economy. “They're struggling with the cost of everything. That's why I'm running,” she said.
STRONG BONDS Reuters/Ipsos polling shows Trump's support among white evangelicals fell to 63% this month from 77% in January 2025. The decline is slightly smaller than his drop among the electorate as a whole, from 47% to 31%, and white evangelicals remain the only major demographic group tracked by Reuters/Ipsos where his support tops 60%.
The thrice-married Trump's bond with white evangelicals has survived a decade of scandals and investigations, including dozens of allegations of [USN:L6N43G12W TEXT:"sexual misconduct"], which he denies, and a [USN:O8N43T00F TEXT:"hush-money case"] involving a porn star. The question for Republicans is whether economic pressures and unhappiness over the Iran war, now in its eighth month, are weakening that bond.
Reuters interviews with 15 people at two South Carolina churches suggested that his hold on white evangelical voters remained strong. At Village Church and Carolina Baptist Church in the city of Spartanburg, about a 90-minute drive from Blythewood, only 2 of the 15 said they were considering Andrews, and none indicated they were abandoning Trump.
While several voiced frustration with the Iran conflict and rising gas prices, most said they [USN:L4N40Q1CN TEXT:"trusted Trump"] to keep Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon or, like Trump, [USN:L1N44A0QY TEXT:"blamed inflation"] on policies enacted under Democratic President Joe Biden.
Chad Connelly, an evangelical activist who heads the Christian voter-engagement group Faith Wins, said that while evangelicals "don't like paying higher prices," they are equally animated by social issues. Concerns about transgender athletes are "really playing everywhere" across the nearly two dozen states he has visited this election cycle, he said.
White evangelicals' loyalty to Trump reflects what Robert P. Jones, president of the Public Religion Research Institute, a nonprofit organization that studies religion and politics, calls a "grand bargain" forged during the 2016 election.
Many evangelicals have overlooked his personal conduct in exchange for his commitment to curtail abortion and LGBTQ rights, advance a conservative Christian vision of American life and pursue strict immigration policies that some supporters see as preserving the country's white Christian identity, Jones said.
"That has proven to be more powerful for this group than what they're having to pay at the gas pump," Jones, who has written extensively about the rise of Christian nationalism in American politics, told Reuters.
WHY EVANGELICALS MATTER White evangelicals make up about 13% of US adults but nearly a third of Trump's winning coalition in 2024, according to a PRRI survey and a validated-voter analysis by the nonpartisan Pew Research Center. More than 80% voted for Trump in each of his three presidential campaigns, according to Pew. They differ sharply from Black Protestant evangelicals, who overwhelmingly support Democrats.
Evangelicals' loyalty could also prove pivotal in Senate races beyond South Carolina that may help determine control of Congress, including in [USN:L6N44F10S TEXT:"Iowa"] and [USN:L6N45Z1B9 TEXT:"Kansas"], where white evangelicals make up a significant share of the electorate.
Opinion polls suggest the race in South Carolina is close. This week Trafalgar Group, a Republican-leaning pollster, released a survey showing Andrews trailing Graham by 3 percentage points.
Part of Graham's challenge stems from lingering unease among some conservatives over her appointment to the Senate seat. Even after a boost from Trump, the political newcomer only narrowly defeated US Representative Ralph Norman in the party's August runoff, underscoring questions among some Republicans about her experience and conservative credentials.
A spokesperson for the Graham campaign did not respond to a request for comment.
Yet even evangelicals lukewarm on Graham, like 53-year-old Kevin Thomas, said they felt they had no choice. Thomas, who attended the Village Church sermon, said he did not trust Andrews on transgender issues, despite a recent campaign ad in which she said she opposed both transgender women competing in women's sports and gender-affirming surgeries for minors.
“I’m leaning towards holding my nose and voting for Graham,” said Thomas, who had backed Norman. "I’m not willing to sacrifice six years of having a Democrat representing us in South Carolina."
items.raw_description: President Donald Trump is losing ground among many of the voters who returned him to the White House in 2024. But Reuters/Ipsos polling and interviews with white evangelical Christians show they remain his most reliable constituency and could prove crucial in the November 3 midterm elections.

items.title: Asia needs $1 trillion investment annually for next 15 years to boost energy security, McKinsey says
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: Asia may need to invest as much as $1 trillion annually in energy over the next 15 years, according to a McKinsey report released on Thursday, as countries seek to strengthen energy security after the Iran war disrupted oil and gas flows through the Strait of Hormuz.
items.body:
Asia may need to invest as much as $1 trillion annually in energy over the next 15 years, according to a McKinsey report released on Thursday, as countries seek to strengthen energy security after the Iran war disrupted oil and gas flows through the Strait of Hormuz.
Here are the key findings:
McKinsey raised its forecast for Asia's energy demand to just under 400 million terajoules, 15% higher than its forecast from a year ago
Asia is expected to drive about 70% of global net energy demand growth through 2040
New sources of energy demand include data centres while requirement from cooling and industrial activities is also rising
Coal is expected to remain a part of Asia's energy mix for longer than previously anticipated, with regional demand seen staying broadly flat over the next decade as declining consumption in China is offset by growth in India and Southeast Asia
Gas demand is set to slow down in the next 5-10 years as countries prioritise coal and renewables for power generation. However, gas consumption could rebound in the longer term driven by industrials
Renewables continue to accelerate particularly in India and Southeast Asia, with about $300 billion in annual solar and wind investment expected through 2040
Focus on energy security could enable the development of higher-cost upstream assets with government support in China, Philippines, Thailand, Vietnam and Turkmenistan
Biofuels could replace about $90 billion to $100 billion in fuel imports in 2026, creating the potential for a longer-term reduction in import dependence
items.raw_description: Asia may need to invest as much as $1 trillion annually in energy over the next 15 years, according to a McKinsey report released on Thursday, as countries seek to strengthen energy security after the Iran war disrupted oil and gas flows through the Strait of Hormuz.

items.title: Trump's tax-exempt diesel draws skepticism from farmers, eludes others
items.author: Tom Polansek
items.creator: Tom Polansek
items.summary: US President Donald Trump signed an executive order this month to expand access to tax-exempt diesel as soaring prices frustrate voters ahead of midterm elections. But farmers say it is too risky to use the fuel on public roads, while some other drivers do not have access to it.
items.body:
US President Donald Trump signed an executive order this month to expand access to tax-exempt diesel as soaring prices frustrate voters ahead of midterm elections. But farmers say it is too risky to use the fuel on public roads, while some other drivers do not have access to it.
Trump has sought to lower prices and boost his sagging approval ratings through a series of actions focused on fuel, including an [USN:L1N466010 TEXT:"$8 billion financial support program"] he announced on Monday to offset diesel costs for farmers during the autumn harvest.
His administration also relaxed sanctions on Russian fuel shipments, pushed allies to release emergency oil stocks and temporarily lifted restrictions on foreign-flagged vessels moving between US ports. Still, prices [USN:L6N45Z19G TEXT:"remain elevated"] because of the US-led war with Iran.
Trump said his [USN:L1N45R0NK TEXT:"executive order"] would temporarily waive an off-road requirement for red-dyed diesel, which is generally sold for use in farm equipment. Red diesel is essentially the same as regular or clear diesel but exempt from highway fuel taxes. It is dyed red to indicate highway taxes have not been paid.
Farmers said potential savings from using dyed diesel in semi-trucks on highways were too small to justify the risk of red residue staying in fuel tanks after the order expires. States have their own taxes and rules for red diesel use, and can fine drivers thousands of dollars if authorities inspect fuel tanks and find signs red diesel was used improperly on public roads.
The Internal Revenue Service said it would not impose a penalty when dyed diesel is used on highways from October 1 to December 31 but that Trump's order had no effect on state taxes and penalties.
"In my mind, it's not anywhere near worth the risk," said Glenn Brunkow, president of the Kansas Farm Bureau, who raises crops and cattle near Wamego, Kansas. "That residue might be in there for years."
FINES UP TO $10,000 IN KANSAS Farmers use the most diesel during the autumn harvest season, burning dyed fuel in tractors, combines and other machinery. Under Trump's order, they could also use red diesel to haul crops to market in semi-trucks normally fueled by clear diesel, if allowed by states.
Kansas, a major grain producer, prohibits using dyed diesel on public roadways unless it is purchased lawfully outside the state. Violators can be charged with a felony, have their driver's license suspended, and face penalties of $1,000 to $10,000, according to the Kansas Department of Revenue.
Governor Laura Kelly, a Democrat, said the state could not legally implement Trump's order as drafted. The Kansas Highway Patrol was concerned it "would result in law enforcement difficulties once red dye diesel returns to its normal usage restrictions," she said in a statement.
Democrats [USN:L6N46610E TEXT:"hope"] surging farm costs can help revive their support in the Republican heartland in November's midterm elections.
Trump wants lower fuel prices, White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers said.
"President Trump remains committed to unleashing American energy dominance, cutting costs, and putting more money back in the pockets of hardworking American families," Rogers said.
For Jay Sorg, a fifth-generation farmer in New Richland, Minnesota, the order could save $1,500 to $2,000, but that is not enough to offset higher costs for fuel and other inputs. Like many farmers, he buys diesel in advance to store in tanks.
"In the grand scheme of our business, it's kind of inconsequential, especially when we already have fuel bought and in the tank for highway use," Sorg said. "It's a move to try to win votes."
Ryan Wagner, a farmer in Roslyn, South Dakota, worried that increasing usage of tax-exempt red diesel could drain government funds used to maintain roads.
"It's a very short-sighted plan that could come back and haunt us in the future," he said.
LIMITED ACCESS For other motorists, it can be hard to get their hands on red diesel.
Iowa Governor Kim Reynolds, a Republican, issued a proclamation that allows vehicles to use dyed diesel on highways until February, but only if they are hauling specific agricultural products.
In Texas, drivers must register with the state to take advantage of a temporary suspension of restrictions on the use of red diesel on highways.
A Reuters reporter visited four sites around Houston that were listed online as selling red diesel by companies that offer fuel cards to commercial operators. Three of the sites sold only commercial diesel, and red diesel pumps at the fourth site were not working. A notice at the fourth site said red diesel was purely for agricultural use and should not be used on roads.
Vincenzo Lasalosi, a firefighter in Houston, said he considered using red diesel in his Ram 2500 truck due to high diesel prices but did not know where to find it.
"Even if I do find it, it's probably too far and not worth the drive to fill it up," he said.

items.title: Singapore's wealthy clients see growing assets over past year, Citi report says
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: Singapore's domestic and overseas wealth pool has expanded steadily over the past year, with average assets among the country's high-net-worth clients rising 6% to $1.5 million, a white paper prepared by Citi Wealth and independent research firm RFI Global showed on Thursday.
items.body:
Singapore's domestic and overseas wealth pool has expanded steadily over the past year, with average assets among the country's high-net-worth clients rising 6% to $1.5 million, a white paper prepared by Citi Wealth and independent research firm RFI Global showed on Thursday.
Assets among Singapore's affluent clients increased 5% to more than $565,000, according to the study, aimed at exploring how Singapore compares with other global wealth markets
The study found that mutual fund ownership among Singapore's high-net-worth investors has nearly tripled from 11% in 2022 to 31% in 2026, the highest adoption level in Asia, outpacing countries like India and South Korea
However, a large portion of portfolios remain held in cash, with 72% of onshore affluent assets and 74% of offshore booked assets concentrated in cash and liquid deposits
The findings were similar across other Asia hubs, reflecting investors' continued preference for liquidity
The study found Singapore leading in intergenerational wealth preparedness, with 76% of individuals aged 55 and above having established wills or wealth succession plans

items.title: Republican backlash over Russia policy poses challenge for Trump in Congress
items.author: Richard Cowan
items.creator: Richard Cowan
items.summary: Bipartisan opposition potentially complicates Trump's agenda.
items.body:
US President Donald Trump's moves in recent weeks to ease economic pressure on Russia while stepping up criticism of Ukraine have triggered bipartisan opposition in Congress, potentially complicating his agenda after next month's midterm elections.
Seeking to draw Russian President Vladimir Putin into negotiations to end the war in Ukraine, Trump has [USN:L4N45Y0AR TEXT:"lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports "]and [USN:FWN4622VQ TEXT:"waived newly enacted sanctions"] against Russian officials, oligarchs, banks and state enterprises.
At the same time, he has increased pressure on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, calling for him to be replaced as the country's leader. A satellite system used by Ukraine for battlefield communications and drone operations was [USN:L1N4610ZC TEXT:"throttled"] following an order from inside the White House, Reuters reported last week.
Seventeen Democrats and five Republicans in the House of Representatives urged Trump in an October 15 letter to "apply the Graham law's sanctions to their fullest extent and without delay." The lawmakers added that Putin "has repeatedly shown that he responds to pressure, not goodwill."
They were referring to legislation, championed by the late Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina, that Congress passed overwhelmingly and Trump signed into law in mid-September.
The Republican signatories were Representatives Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, Joe Wilson of South Carolina, Michael McCaul of Texas, Don Bacon of Nebraska and Dan Newhouse of Washington state.
The backlash could pose new hurdles for Trump after the November 3 midterm elections, when Congress takes up defense and spending bills that lawmakers could use to try to reverse or alter his Russia policies.
Fitzpatrick went further. In a post on X on Monday he wrote that any move to [USN:L1N464034 TEXT:"limit the use of "Starshield""] intelligence to warn Kyiv of Russian attacks would be "fully investigated" by Congress with "harsh and punitive budget cuts to any responsible agency or agency head."
The White House pushed back in an email to Reuters:
“President Trump has been clear that he wants to see this brutal war come to an end," White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said, adding that Trump "retains the ability to exercise these authorities at any time if he determines that doing so would advance national interests."
PROSPECT OF BIPARTISAN OPPOSITION TO TRUMP'S PRIORITIES The pushback has raised the possibility that some Republican lawmakers could join Democrats in investigations and legislation reversing Trump's priorities following the midterm elections.
Congress' post-election work includes attempts to pass a bill authorizing defense programs for another year and across-the-board government spending through September 30, 2027, that includes appropriations for the Pentagon and intelligence agencies.
If Congress uses those bills to try to change his Russia policies, Trump could veto them, setting up a showdown.
James Lindsay, a US foreign policy expert at the Council on Foreign Relations, said the Republican backlash was not surprising given the Senate's bipartisan votes on the Graham bill.
But passing legislation faces major challenges, Lindsay said.
"Even if Congress can overcome its institutional divisions, its partisan divisions and overcome a presidential veto ... that's no guarantee the president will act or observe that constraint," he said.
REPUBLICANS BACKING TRUMP Despite the growing pushback, many Republicans are backing Trump.
Republican Senator Ted Budd told Reuters at a Trump rally in his home state of North Carolina that he supports the president's pivot toward Putin, saying the recent agreement on Russian diesel sales was important to keep Moscow involved in negotiations to end its war with Ukraine.
"It's a very minimal dollar amount actually to Russia, but it's enough of a fig leaf to get them to the table to bring an end to the aggression against Ukraine," said Budd, an Armed Services Committee member.
The elections, which will determine whether Republicans hold their narrow House and Senate majorities, could influence the way legislative battles between the two parties, and with Trump, turn out.
Trump is not on the ballot, but the elections are widely seen as a referendum on his presidency. Voters are on edge over rising consumer prices and the war with Iran.
An [USN:L1N45Z0TJ TEXT:"October 13 letter"] to Trump signed by five senior Senate Republicans, along with six Democrats, also criticized his diesel agreement.
House Speaker Mike Johnson, a staunch supporter of Trump, has even hinted at his discomfort with current Russia policy.
Asked on Fox News' Sunday Morning Futures program whether he supported Trump's decision to waive the Russia sanctions, Johnson said: "Congress voted on this decisively." He added that he was in discussions with Republican members of the Foreign Affairs and Intelligence committees.
"We understand that Putin cannot be trusted," Johnson said and added that he told White House officials: "We need to talk about it and I think carefully consider the unintended consequences that may ensue" from putting the new Russia sanctions on hold.

[チューリヒ／ロンドン ２２日] -

[チューリヒ／ロンドン ２２日] - スイスの製薬大手ロシュが２２日発表した第３・四半期売上高は、市場予想を上回った。「オクレバス」など主力薬の需要が堅調だった。

グループ売上高は為替変動の影響を除くベースで７％増の１６１億３０００万スイスフラン（１９６億１０００万ドル）となり、同社がまとめた市場予想の１５７億５０００万フラン（１９１億５０００万ドル）を上回った。

ただ競争圧力の兆しも表れた。大型薬「ゾレア」は初の安価な後続品が発売された影響で、売上高が８億４８００万フラン（１０億３０００万ドル）と、市場予想の９億２５００万フラン（１１億２０００万ドル）を下回った。

株価は午前の取引で１．１％下落した。

診断部門の売上高は５％増の３５億４０００万フラン（４３億ドル）で、経営陣は、来年は１桁台半ばから後半の「通常」の伸びに戻る見通しだとした。中国市場について、医療価格改革による下押し圧力は和らいでいると指摘した。

ドルの対スイスフラン相場が安定しつつあることもロシュに追い風となった。グループ売上高の半分近くを占める北米市場で、長引いていた為替の悪影響が和らいだ。

医薬品部門は主力薬がけん引した。中でも多発性硬化症の注射薬オクレバスは、売上高が為替変動の影響を除くベースで９％増の１８億４０００万フラン（２２億４０００万ドル）となった。

items.title: Mapping the Market: Colgate-Palmolive shares look ready to extend rally
items.author: Christopher Romano
items.creator: Christopher Romano
items.summary: Shares in Colgate-Palmolive have gained more than 13% over the last three weeks or so. That rise could be a sign of building momentum for another leg higher, technical analysis suggests.
items.body:
Shares in Colgate-Palmolive (CL.N) have gained more than 13% over the last three weeks or so. That rise could be a sign of building momentum for another leg higher, technical analysis suggests.
Click here for a detailed technical analysis chart.
Technical analysis uses charts of past price moves to map out where a market might go next. Over the years, market watchers have come to recognize that certain chart patterns tend to come before gains.
Colgate's chart has formed one of them, known as a bull pennant, because it resembles the object that flies above baseball stadiums. It is called a continuation pattern because it usually forms between two rally phases in a stock.
The pattern begins with a sharp climb, which forms its vertical part, known as the flagpole. Eventually the shares pause. Analysts call this resting phase consolidation. It happens when some buyers take profits while other investors position themselves for fresh gains.
During consolidation the stock moves little in either direction. Lines connecting its highs and lows converge into a symmetrical triangle that narrows from both sides. The pattern is confirmed when the stock breaks above the triangle's upper line. That is what happened last week, when Colgate shares reached $95.33, highest in about 2-1/2 months, according to LSEG data.
After a breakout, analysts estimate potential gains by measuring the height of the flagpole. For Colgate, that points to a target of $106 and possibly as high as $109.
On the way up, analysts look for chart levels that could act as support -- which works like a floor for prices -- and resistance, which is a ceiling or cap on gains.
They also use tools that measure volatility and momentum to back up their view. Volatility is how much a stock's price swings. Momentum reflects how strongly a stock is moving in one direction.
One such tool is Bollinger Bands. These are two lines drawn above and below a moving average of the stock's price. A moving average smooths out price swings by averaging prices over a set period. The bands widen when price swings grow larger.
Another is Moving Average Convergence Divergence, or MACD. It compares two moving averages of different lengths to show whether buying pressure is building or fading. A third is the Relative Strength Index, or RSI. It gauges the speed of recent price changes to show whether a stock is gaining or losing strength.
All three tools suggest Colgate is gaining upward momentum. Even so, the shares could slow near resistance around $100 on their way higher.
If the shares start to retreat, a fall below support in the $88 to $90 area would probably end the rally for now.
Colgate-Palmolive did not respond to a request for comment.
What the chart shows:
Colgate has gained more than 13% in three weeks and broke out of a bull pennant pattern, hitting $95.33
Gains could target $106 and possibly $109, with resistance near $100 along the way
A fall below support in the $88 to $90 area would likely end the rally for now
(Mapping the Market is a daily column written by Reuters journalists. The commentary is based on a technical analysis of financial charts, which helps assess the likelihood of future price moves but does not guarantee the outcome. The column does not constitute investment advice or trading recommendations. )

items.summary: El Banco Central del Paraguay y su presidente han enfrentado crecientes pedidos de renuncia en las últimas semanas, a medida que se intensifica el escrutinio sobre cómo supervisaron un banco digital de rápido crecimiento con vínculos políticos.
items.body:
El Banco Central del Paraguay y su presidente han enfrentado crecientes pedidos de renuncia en las últimas semanas, a medida que se intensifica el escrutinio sobre cómo supervisaron un banco digital de rápido crecimiento con vínculos políticos.
Senadores del partido gobernante y de la oposición han instado al presidente, Santiago Peña, a destituir a la cúpula de la banca matriz, en un caso que está poniendo a prueba la reputación que ayudó a Paraguay a convertirse en uno de los destinos emergentes de Sudamérica para el capital extranjero, gran parte del cual proviene de Brasil.
Las autoridades intentaron insistentemente las últimas semanas calmar al mercado financiero después de que se conociera que los directores de ueno, un banco de capital mayoritariamente local que administra más de 800 millones de dólares en fondos públicos, estaban bajo un sumario administrativo por una operación de venta de cartera.
Ueno pasó de ser una empresa local de tecnología financiera de nicho a convertirse en un banco de tamaño medio, con cerca de 3 millones de clientes, en la línea de plataformas digitales como Monzo y Nubank.
"El cambio de las autoridades del Banco Central debe hacerse y lo antes posible. Es necesario cuando hay rumores que estos sean evacuados rápidamente. La gente del BCP perdió credibilidad", afirmó a Reuters el senador oficialista Gustavo Leite.
Los detalles de la investigación preliminar figuran en un informe que el Banco Central envió este mes al Senado, que buscaba despejar dudas sobre los préstamos de ueno a empresas vinculadas pero terminó avivando los cuestionamientos de legisladores, el gremio de bancos y otras agrupaciones empresariales.
"Hay muchas señales de alerta con relación a esa entidad (...) que el Banco Central no aclara. El sistema financiero está sufriendo un daño tremendo", señaló por su parte el senador opositor Rafael Filizzola, que presentó esta semana otro pedido de informe sobre ueno.
La Asociación de Bancos del Paraguay integrada por 14 bancos privados, entre ellos Itaú [RIC:RIC:ITUBK.UL] y GNB [RIC:RIC:GNBI.UL], dijo en un comunicado el fin de semana que las respuestas del Banco Central "son incompletas y dejan dudas" y que la solvencia de una entidad "no puede depender de un trato distinto al que reciben las demás".
VÍNCULOS POLÍTICOS El caso es políticamente delicado.
El presidente del Banco Central, Carlos Carvallo, trabajó anteriormente en ueno y ocupó el cargo de presidente de la entidad hasta agosto de 2023, confirmó la empresa a Reuters.
Peña fue socio comercial del grupo propietario del banco hasta marzo de 2025. Ueno afirmó que el actual mandatario nunca mantuvo relación alguna con el banco en calidad de accionista o inversor.
Gran parte de la presión para obtener respuestas provino de senadores del Partido Colorado, al que pertenece Peña, en medio de una disputa política por la candidatura presidencial para las elecciones generales del 2028.
En una respuesta escrita a Reuters, el Banco Central describió la situación actual como "política-mediática" y negó que haya un conflicto de intereses ya que Carvallo "se ha inhibido en cada decisión vinculada a Ueno Bank (...) más aún, personalmente optó por retirarse de sala cada vez que se discutía o analizaba cualquier caso vinculado a la entidad".
La presidencia paraguaya no respondió a un pedido de comentarios. En declaraciones a medios locales a comienzos de octubre, Peña describió la situación como un "desborde" de una cuestión técnica que se llevó al ámbito político y "ha hecho un daño tremendo a la imagen de todo el país".
Ueno confirmó a Reuters que se enfrenta a un procedimiento administrativo preliminar y que el asunto sigue en fase de investigación. La empresa señaló que el procedimiento "no constituye una constatación de irregularidad ni una sanción" y que seguirá "colaborando plenamente" con el Banco Central.
El caso de ueno puso bajo el foco la estabilidad en la pequeña economía del país, que ha captado importantes volúmenes de capital extranjero en los últimos dos años después de alcanzar por primera vez el grado de inversión y espera un crecimiento económico de 5% este año, mayor al promedio de la región.
Entre enero y agosto, los bancos en Paraguay ganaron unos 680 millones de dólares.
